The Sixth Amendment. Ratified in 1791, this part of the Bill of Rights establishes fundamental protections for criminal defendants in the United States. It guarantees the rights to speedy and public trial, confrontation with accusers, compulsory process to obtain witnesses, and crucially, representation by counsel. The amendment's text guarantees the assistance of counsel for a defendant's defense, though courts initially interpreted this as merely the right to hire a lawyer rather than the right to receive one at public expense. This changed with Gideon v. Wainwright in 1963, which held that states must provide counsel to indigent defendants, establishing that the Sixth Amendment requires publicly-funded defense lawyers. The speedy trial right protects defendants from indefinite delay, though courts must balance this against the defense's need for preparation time. Delays exceeding seventy months have been deemed unconstitutional. The confrontation clause permits defendants to cross-examine witnesses, a practice dating to English common law that the amendment constitutionalizes as an ancient protection against secret testimony. The compulsory process clause allows defendants to subpoena witnesses in their favor, shifting power from prosecution to defense in witness acquisition. The jury trial right, paired with the Sixth Amendment, requires that juries be composed of peers and be reasonably informed, establishing jury composition standards and discovery obligations. Through landmark cases like Gideon and Miranda v. Arizona, which established suspects' right to counsel before questioning, the Sixth Amendment has become the constitutional foundation for criminal justice fairness and the development of professional defense counsel systems throughout American jurisprudence.
